## Summary

An OpenAI Core Experimentation engineer's first-person account of turning maintenance from a static-analysis problem into an **agentic evidence-gathering problem**. Three workflows:

- **Dead code.** A deliberately vague prompt ("identify and clean up dead code… feel free to check Slack, Statsig, or any other source") was too ambiguous for GPT-5.6 Sol but Astra handled it: read past PRs, pulled context from Slack threads and internal trackers, checked **production performance profiling tables** to confirm deleted lines were never reached, and explained each deletion's rationale. Five engineers, two weeks, part-time: **1,400+ merged PRs, 800k+ lines deleted**; one container image 3.31GB → 1.72GB (−48%).
- **Stale experiments.** The mature version: engineer + Astra **co-wrote the prompt** (a /goal with safeguards: preserve killswitches, ignore SDK fallbacks, one small draft PR per cleanup, evidence attached). Astra then drafted an even broader whole-repo audit prompt itself, and surfaced a years-old "Permanent" flag whose single inconspicuous mapping line caused major CPU fan-out — it quantified the cost but **escalated to human review instead of deleting**, because the flag was marked permanent. 0.42% CPU saving after review.
- **Flaky tests + CI load.** Short prompts ("look at recent CI runs, find flaky tests, try simple fixes, PR each") → ~30 CI optimization PRs; median CI 10 min → 4.5 min, p90 12.5 → 6. One missing mock cut a 63-test suite 592.6s → 29.8s (−95%).

**The model economics are the quiet headline:** on the same stale-experiment audit (~6k files, 1M+ LOC), **GPT-6.1 Sol Ultra found 92% as many accepted findings as GPT-6 Astra Ultra at 14% of the API cost.** Their response: study the gap (Sol missed flags used as dependencies in other flags), patch the prompt, and re-benchmark on every model release since new models obsolete old prompt fixes. Recommended on-ramp: one small task, compare model/effort tiers on it, scale to a subdirectory, then the codebase — folding review feedback into the next prompt at each step.

## Why it matters

- **First-party evidence that agent-driven maintenance scales.** 1,400 merged PRs and −800k LOC with review acceleration (evidence attached per PR) is the largest public dataset on this workflow shape — validates the backlog-burn pattern we keep capturing from individual practitioners, now from a shop with production telemetry to verify against.
- **Verification against production, not just the repo.** The old way (static analysis + runtime logging) failed on reflection, activatable dead paths, eligibility-dependent experiments. Astra's replacement loop — Slack threads + Statsig state + profiling tables + git history — is exactly the multi-source evidence discipline that separates safe deletion from incident creation (they say mistaken removals caused several incidents pre-agents).
- **The escalation judgment matters more than the deletion.** The "Permanent" killswitch-flag story is the note's core lesson: the agent quantified the win but deferred the decision to a human because the artifact was explicitly marked operational. That boundary-drawing is what we want from our own agents (draft-and-show posture).
- **Cheap-model-first is now OpenAI's own advice.** 92% of findings at 14% of cost, with prompt patches closing known gap patterns — mirrors our own compute-cap thinking, and [[2026-08-30-codex-sol-scope-guard-rules]] (Sol's over-engineering habit, scope-guard rules): the blog even concedes some proposals "added more complexity than their expected benefit justified," so prioritization and measurement stayed in the loop.
- **Directly relevant to our own tooling.** We self-host agents that maintain code (bridge daemons, vault scripts). The flaky-CI and dead-code prompts are copy-paste candidates for a bounded maintenance pass, and the graduated on-ramp (small task → subdir → repo) is how to try it without betting the codebase.
- **Skepticism gates:** single vendor narrating its own models' wins on its own codebase — no failure modes quantified (how many of the 1,400+ PRs were rejected/reverted?), the "92% at 14% cost" is one audit on one repo, and the post is also a hiring pitch for the team (last paragraph). Prompt excerpts are curated by the author, not the raw transcripts.
